items.title: Cavs vs Oklahoma City Thunder
Iran says tankers hit mines in the Strait of Hormuz as the U.S. insists the main lanes are clear
items.summary:
Iran's Revolutionary Guards said on Friday that three oil tankers caught fire after striking naval mines in the Strait of Hormuz, and Iran's regular army reported a fourth vessel ablaze east of the strait. Tehran said all four ships were traveling a southern route near the Omani coast that it considers unauthorized. In a separate incident, the UK Maritime Trade Operations agency said a small boat attached two explosive devices to a tanker's hull about 25 nautical miles northeast of Khasab, Oman, sparking an engine-room fire; the crew was safe and the ship later continued on its way. Oman's navy evacuated 25 crew members from a Panama-flagged merchant vessel that caught fire off Musandam.

The claims land a day after U.S. Central Command said American forces had cleared the strait's internationally recognized primary transit routes of Iranian sea mines and that commercial ships were moving freely. CENTCOM chief Admiral Brad Cooper repeated that message Friday, while an IRGC spokesman demanded independent proof and said the reality in the strait is decided on the water, not on social media. The Iranian mine claims have not been independently verified, and the Guards also said they stopped two more tankers that had tried the southern route with their navigation systems switched off.

The strait normally carries about a fifth of the world's oil and gas, but traffic has fallen to single digits a day since the war began in late February and the conflict is now in its ninth month. Brent crude pushed toward $117 a barrel on Friday, on course for a fourth straight monthly gain, so every disputed incident in the waterway feeds straight into fuel prices far beyond the region — including at the pump in Ohio.

Watch for any independent confirmation of the mine strikes, and for whether tanker traffic through the main lanes holds up over the weekend.

items.title: U.S. approves $2.1 billion sale of 500 Patriot missiles to Ukraine, but delivery could take years
items.summary:
The U.S. State Department has approved a possible sale of 500 Patriot PAC-3 interceptor missiles to Ukraine, a package valued at about $2.1 billion. The missiles are the most capable air-defense interceptors Kyiv has for stopping Russian ballistic missiles, and Ukraine has been warning for weeks that its stocks are running critically low as Russia steps up strikes on cities and energy infrastructure ahead of winter.

No U.S. government money is involved: the purchase is to be paid for by Ukraine's partners, with Canada, Germany and Norway contributing through the JUMPSTART program and national funds backed by an EU Ukraine Support Loan. Lockheed Martin is the principal contractor, and the approval now goes to Congress for review. The catch is timing — the missiles would be newly manufactured rather than drawn from existing stock, and President Volodymyr Zelensky warned Friday night that deliveries could take several years, renewing his appeal for Washington to speed up supplies already promised.

The announcement follows a rocky stretch between Kyiv and Washington, including President Trump's suggestion that Ukraine needed new leadership, before relations eased after Zelensky met U.S. envoys in Oslo on October 20. For Ukraine, the deal is a long-term promise of protection rather than help for this winter's air campaign.

Watch the congressional review period, and whether any interceptors from existing allied stockpiles are released in the meantime.

items.title: Europeans snub Russia's Lavrov at the G20 in Atlanta, and the group photo is cancelled
items.summary:
Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov's return to a G20 gathering on U.S. soil turned into a public cold shoulder in Atlanta. European ministers, along with Britain and Australia, refused to stand for the traditional group photograph alongside Lavrov, and host Secretary of State Marco Rubio cancelled the photo altogether rather than let it become the story of the meeting. UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband told Lavrov directly in the room that everyone knows who the aggressor in Ukraine is, and EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said European officials challenged a stream of Russian falsehoods face to face.

Lavrov, who remains under international sanctions and last attended a G20 in Johannesburg in February 2025, held his own press conference attacking European governments for an arrogant boycott while praising the Trump administration for engaging with Moscow. Rubio did hold a brief sideline conversation with him, underscoring the split: Washington is restoring diplomatic contact with the Kremlin — President Trump has invited Vladimir Putin to Florida in December and fresh three-way talks are expected in November — while European capitals insist Russia cannot be treated as a normal partner while the invasion continues.

The two-day meeting was officially about growth, energy security, trade, freedom of navigation in the Black Sea and the Strait of Hormuz, and food supply chains. The Lavrov dispute shows how far apart the U.S. and its European allies now are on the basic question of how to handle Russia, even as they sit at the same table.

The meeting wraps up Saturday; watch for a joint statement — or the lack of one — on Ukraine and energy security.

items.title: Congo's Ebola outbreak passes 5,000 deaths, the country's deadliest on record
items.summary:
The death toll from the Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo has passed 5,000, according to government figures released Friday — 5,026 confirmed deaths out of 10,351 confirmed cases as of October 29, a fatality rate near 49 percent. The outbreak, declared in May, is driven by the rare Bundibugyo strain of the virus, for which there are no approved vaccines or treatments.

Eight of Congo's 26 provinces and 67 health zones are affected, concentrated in Ituri and North Kivu in the east, and many deaths are occurring outside treatment centers. Health officials say roughly 80 percent of new infections are appearing outside the contact chains they are monitoring, which makes containment far harder; about 2,788 patients have recovered so far. It is now the second-largest Ebola epidemic ever recorded, behind only the 2014–2016 West Africa outbreak that killed more than 11,000 people.

The spread is becoming an international concern: cases have been reported in neighboring countries, Saudi Arabia suspended travel to and from Kenya on Friday, and the U.S. CDC has set a 21-day travel restriction policy for people arriving from Congo to take effect November 3 through mid-December.

Watch whether funding and staffing for contact tracing surge in the coming week — officials say that, more than anything, decides whether this keeps growing.

items.title: Qatar works to restart direct U.S.–Iran talks, with reports of 'positive progress'
items.summary:
Qatari mediators have spent more than 12 hours in talks aimed at renewing direct negotiations between the United States and Iran, according to reports citing Axios and regional outlets. A diplomatic source said the mediators stayed in contact with the White House during Friday's discussions and described positive progress toward getting the two sides back to the table, with an American delegation expected to join the Qatar-hosted discussions with Iranian representatives.

The diplomatic push runs in parallel with the military standoff in the Strait of Hormuz, where Iran says tankers are still hitting mines and Washington says the main lanes are cleared. Details of what is actually being discussed remain unconfirmed and partly conflicting — one Saudi channel aired alleged terms that have not been verified — and U.S. military sources have signaled contingency planning for a possible resumption of operations after Tuesday's midterm elections.

That mix is the story of this conflict in its ninth month: talking and threatening at the same time. A credible direct channel would be the first real off-ramp either side has had in months, but similar openings have collapsed before.

Watch for an official statement from Doha or Washington confirming a direct meeting, rather than another round of mediated messages.

items.title: A third U.S. aircraft carrier heads toward the Iran theater as Trump says the conflict will 'get wrapped up soon'
items.summary:
The United States is sending a third aircraft carrier toward the Middle East as the war with Iran grinds through its ninth month, even as President Trump publicly suggests the conflict will be wrapped up soon. The deployment adds naval air power to a region where the fight over the Strait of Hormuz — the world's most important oil chokepoint — has become the central front.

The move comes alongside two other escalatory signals this week: the U.S. ordered non-emergency government staff and their families to leave Saudi Arabia over security risks, citing Houthi attacks on civilian airports and infrastructure, and the Army has been running mass-casualty preparation exercises. At the same time, Qatari mediators are working to restart direct U.S.–Iran negotiations, so the carrier surge reads as pressure designed to shape a deal as much as preparation for more fighting.

More carriers in the region raise both deterrence and risk. Any miscalculation around the strait, where tankers are already being attacked, could widen the war quickly — one reason oil markets are pricing Brent near $117 a barrel.

Watch whether the carrier's arrival coincides with a negotiating breakthrough or with the post-election resumption of strikes that some U.S. military sources have hinted at.

items.title: Congress campaign enters its final weekend: record early voting, an Alaska investigation, and lawsuits everywhere
items.summary:
The fight for control of Congress reached its final weekend with early voting at a midterm record — nearly 50 million Americans have already cast ballots, up from about 46 million at this point in 2022, according to the University of Florida's Election Lab. All 435 House seats and 35 Senate seats are on Tuesday's ballot, with Republicans defending narrow majorities in both chambers and polls favoring Democrats to take the House, with a plausible path to the Senate as well.

The sharpest fight is in Alaska, one of the closest Senate races in the country. The Justice Department accelerated a criminal investigation Friday into reports that aides to a Democratic candidate recruited a retired schoolteacher named Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. — a nonpartisan candidate who shares a name with Republican incumbent Sen. Dan S. Sullivan — to siphon votes. The U.S. attorney in Alaska called it a sham-candidate scheme at a Friday press conference, and the department, acting on a civil suit President Trump says he instigated, also moved to block Alaska from certifying the result if the incumbent loses narrowly. Democrats need Alaska if they are to flip the Senate.

The administration is intervening in races nationwide at the same time — it has sued California over roughly 20,000 ballots it says may belong to noncitizens, a case it lost twice this week — while a bipartisan 76 percent of voters still say they are confident their ballots will be counted accurately. President Trump, after cancelling in-person rallies in Kansas and Iowa, returns to the trail Sunday in both states and is running a 72-hour tele-rally push into nearly 20 states.

Everything now runs through Tuesday: watch Alaska, the California ballot litigation, and whether the Democrats' polling lead survives contact with Election Day turnout.

items.title: Judge orders the Justice Department to stop threatening election officials over voter rolls
items.summary:
A federal judge on Friday ordered the Trump administration's Justice Department to stop threatening to prosecute state and local election officials who refuse its demands on voting by alleged noncitizens. U.S. District Judge Trina Thompson issued a temporary restraining order in a lawsuit brought by election workers' unions and other groups, finding that with the election only days away, the balance of equities and the public interest favored the officials on the ground.

The order bars the department from demanding that local officials remove voters from statewide rolls, refuse ballots to specific voters, or segregate ballots in the midterms based on the administration's lists of alleged noncitizen voters. The Justice Department had no immediate comment. The ruling is the administration's second courtroom loss on election intervention this week, after an appeals court again refused to let it set aside more than 20,000 California mail ballots.

The administration says its aggressive election oversight is about security and public confidence. Critics, including election officials from both parties, call it federal overreach into elections the Constitution leaves to the states — and judges, so far, are mostly agreeing with the critics.

The restraining order runs through the election; watch for an administration appeal and for how states handle any late federal demands this weekend.

items.title: Three days out, the midterms are being decided by grocery bills and corruption fears
items.summary:
With the November 3 midterms three days away, national polling gives Democrats a clear edge: RealClearPolling's averages put them ahead 51.4 percent to 43.2 percent on the generic ballot, an 8.2-point lead, and President Trump's approval has fallen to 37–38 percent with disapproval around 60 percent. Democrats need a net gain of just three seats to take the House, where Republicans hold 219 seats to 214, and four to reach a 51-seat Senate majority.

What voters say is driving them is not subtle. A Harris poll finds the cost of living is the top concern for 36 percent of likely voters, 42 percent say they are financially worse off than a year ago, and government corruption has jumped to second place at 12 percent — ahead of immigration at 9 percent. A striking 76 percent believe elected officials put self-enrichment ahead of the public, and campaign ad spending has hit a record $11.2 billion trying to move those numbers.

The Senate map shows the strain: Democratic challenger James Talarico leads Republican Ken Paxton 49–43 in Texas in recent CNN polling, and Democrat Abdul El-Sayed leads Republican Mike Rogers 49–42 in Michigan. Those are states Republicans expected to hold.

Watch the late-deciding independents — about 5 percent remain undecided, most of them independents who lean against the president, which is why both parties are flooding the same handful of states this weekend.

items.title: Trump's approval is net-positive in only 8 states heading into the midterms
items.summary:
President Trump's job approval is underwater in 42 of 50 states just days before the midterms, according to the latest Civiqs state-by-state tracker. He remains net-positive only in Alabama, Arkansas, Idaho, North Dakota, Oklahoma, Utah, West Virginia and Wyoming — all states he carried in each of the last three presidential elections — with Wyoming his strongest at plus-14 and Kansas exactly even.

The damaging part for Republicans is where the negatives are deepest: every one of the six swing states with tight Senate races is well underwater, including Alaska at minus-25, Michigan at minus-26, Maine at minus-29, North Carolina at minus-18, Ohio at minus-18 and Texas at minus-20. A new Emerson College poll on Friday put Trump's national approval at 37 percent, the lowest of his second term in that survey, alongside a 10-point Democratic lead on the generic congressional ballot.

Presidents' approval ratings are the single best predictor of midterm losses, which is why these numbers have Republicans bracing and Democrats talking about a wave. Emerson's polling director noted that most of the remaining undecided voters are independents, half of whom disapprove of Trump — meaning the Democrats' ceiling could be higher than the headline numbers.

Watch whether Trump's Sunday rallies in Kansas and Iowa and his tele-rally blitz move late numbers at all — at this point, most of the electorate has already voted or decided.

items.title: Maine's Senate race is the most expensive per person in America, and voters are feeling it
items.summary:
Maine's Senate race between five-term Republican Sen. Susan Collins and Democrat Troy Jackson, the former state Senate president, has drawn nearly $218 million in broadcast advertising — about $160 for every person in the state, the highest per-capita figure of any competitive Senate race, according to a USA Today analysis of AdImpact data from October 28. Republicans are outspending Democrats by about $305 million across the competitive Senate races nationally, in what is shaping up as the most expensive election cycle in U.S. history.

Collins is in a uniquely exposed spot: she is the only Republican running for re-election in a state Trump lost in 2024. On doorsteps, canvassers say the conversation is less about the ads than about affordability — Maine has New England's lowest median income, and heating-oil costs are up roughly 80 percent from a year ago as winter sets in. Jackson blames the Iran war for choking oil supply; Collins blames Jackson's years leading the state legislature for driving up electricity costs.

Small, cheap-media states are where record national money goes furthest, which is why Maine and Alaska — at $140 per person — top the per-capita chart ahead of far bigger battlegrounds like Texas at $14.

Watch whether the spending gap translates on Tuesday, and whether Collins's personal brand in Maine can still beat the national environment.

items.title: Trump puts Kansas and Iowa rallies back on for Sunday after cancelling them
items.summary:
President Trump has put in-person rallies in Kansas and Iowa back on his schedule for Sunday, November 1, two days before the midterms, after abruptly cancelling both events earlier in the week, a Republican source told AFP on Friday. The reversal restores the traditional closing-weekend swing through two states where Republicans are defending vulnerable Senate seats, including Sen. Roger Marshall's tough re-election fight in Kansas.

The whiplash is the second schedule change in days: Trump had also cancelled a planned Salina, Kansas appearance set for Halloween and shifted to a 72-hour tele-rally format aimed at nearly 20 states. Vice President JD Vance has been carrying the in-person load in the region, rallying in Topeka on October 26 and making the closing argument Friday that a Democratic win would open the border, sharing video of migrants moving through Mexico who said they hoped Democratic victories would soften Trump's immigration policies.

Closing weekends are about base turnout, not persuasion, and both parties know it — with nearly 50 million votes already cast, the rallies are aimed at the slice of supporters who still vote on the day itself.

Watch the Sunday crowds in Kansas and Iowa, and whether any other cancelled stops quietly come back onto the schedule.

items.title: Wall Street's AI selloff deepens: Nasdaq's worst day since June, Intel down 29 percent
items.summary:
U.S. stocks closed sharply lower Friday as investors bailed out of the artificial-intelligence trade. The Nasdaq Composite fell 2.86 percent to 25,437 — its biggest one-day drop since June 5 and now down 7.8 percent from its October 6 record close — while the S&P 500 lost 1.82 percent to 7,580 and the Dow fell 1.09 percent to 51,770. It was the technology sector's worst month since March 2025.

Intel was the epicenter, plunging 28.6 percent after a weak outlook tied to soft PC demand and shutdowns at its plant in Israel, erasing roughly $140 billion in value in its worst session since the 1970s. The damage spread across the chip complex: Nvidia fell 4.2 percent, AMD dropped 10.9 percent, the semiconductor index lost 7.2 percent, and server makers Dell and HP fell about 10 percent each. Amazon's results added to the gloom, crypto stocks slid 7 to 11 percent after the Binance hack, and energy, staples, utilities and health care were the only real shelter. Beneath the panic, earnings season itself is strong — 82 percent of the 299 S&P 500 companies that have reported beat estimates, with profits up about 31.6 percent.

The argument on Wall Street is no longer whether AI works; it is whether the hundreds of billions being spent on it will earn their keep fast enough to justify the prices investors paid in September.

Watch Monday's open for whether Friday was capitulation or the start of a deeper repricing — and the next round of big-tech spending forecasts.

items.title: The $6.3 billion Binance hack: North Korea's TraderTraitor blamed for crypto's biggest theft
items.summary:
Attackers drained about $6.36 billion from Binance, the world's largest crypto exchange, on Thursday evening — most of it in roughly 20 minutes starting at 4:05 p.m. Eastern, across ten blockchains including Bitcoin, Ethereum, Solana and Tron. Blockchain intelligence firm TRM Labs, which tracked the flows, calls it the largest cryptocurrency theft on record, more than four times the $1.5 billion Bybit hack of February 2025.

TRM attributes the attack with high confidence to TraderTraitor, North Korea's elite state hacking unit — the same group the FBI blamed for Bybit — and Chainalysis publicly agreed with the assessment. Binance says the breach began with a compromised DevOps engineer's laptop, which gave the attackers access to a service container used to submit unauthorized withdrawals; it found no evidence wallet private keys leaked, though investigators later found additional points of breach. On Ethereum, the attacker used a technical delegation trick to turn a Binance hot wallet into a sweeper under their control, with 50 pre-signed authorizations prepared in advance.

Binance and its partners, including Tether and Circle, have frozen roughly $3 billion of the stolen assets, deposits were never affected, withdrawals are paused and expected to resume within a day or two, and the exchange says its SAFU fund will cover all losses. U.S. intelligence has assessed that Pyongyang nets at least $1 billion a year from crypto theft to fund its weapons programs — which is what makes a $6.3 billion haul a national-security story, not just a market one.

Watch the laundering trail: how much of the unfrozen half starts moving, and whether exchanges worldwide tighten withdrawal controls in response.

items.title: FBI joins the Binance response as the North Korea link hardens
items.summary:
The FBI confirmed Friday that it is working with government and industry partners on the Binance theft, saying it is engaged to understand the scope of the activity, evaluate potential impacts and coordinate investigative steps. The bureau stopped short of attributing the attack to North Korea itself, but the private sector has been less cautious: TRM Labs and Chainalysis both tie the heist to TraderTraitor, Pyongyang's premier hacking unit.

The speed of the federal response reflects what is at stake. At an estimated $6.3 billion, this single theft is several times the roughly $1 billion a year U.S. intelligence believes North Korea steals in crypto to finance its government and weapons programs. Microsoft Threat Intelligence added a worrying layer on Thursday, warning that North Korean groups are increasingly using AI to research victims, build convincing fake identities and scale phishing — the kind of social engineering that likely put the malware on the engineer's laptop at the center of this breach.

For everyday crypto holders, the practical takeaway is that the exchange, not users, absorbed the loss this time — Binance has promised to cover everything and freeze what can be frozen. The policy fight that follows will be about whether the biggest exchanges face bank-style security obligations.

Watch for a formal FBI attribution statement, which would set up sanctions and possible indictments in the weeks ahead.

items.title: DoorDash agrees to buy Instacart for $17 billion in delivery's biggest deal
items.summary:
DoorDash announced a definitive agreement to acquire Instacart for $65.00 a share — a deal valued at about $17 billion, at least 75 percent cash and up to 25 percent stock, representing a 26 percent premium to Instacart's October 22 closing price. It is the biggest deal yet in food delivery, and it lands months after Uber's roughly $15 billion purchase of Delivery Hero reset the industry's map.

The announcement came wrapped inside a record quarter: DoorDash's third-quarter orders rose 28 percent to 993 million, marketplace volume jumped 36 percent to $33.9 billion, revenue grew 34 percent to $4.6 billion, and net income nearly doubled to $466 million. Management says combining DoorDash's logistics network with Instacart's grocery software and retailer relationships should produce $500 million or more in annual synergies, all of which it plans to reinvest in the first year — and Instacart's technology is used by grocers who compete with DoorDash's own marketplace, which is precisely the point.

The deal is expected to close by the first half of 2028 and will face serious antitrust scrutiny: the FTC has been focused on delivery-app fees and affordability, and this merger would put restaurant delivery and the largest grocery-delivery network under one roof.

Watch the FTC's posture over the coming months, and how Walmart and Amazon — Instacart partners and DoorDash rivals — respond.

items.title: AI spending is eating shareholder returns: buybacks at five tech giants fall 83 percent
items.summary:
The five biggest U.S. tech companies — Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon, Meta and Oracle — returned just 9.3 percent of the cash their businesses generated to shareholders in the first nine months of 2026, down from 27.4 percent a year earlier and the lowest share in 15 years, according to Reuters data. Buybacks collapsed 83 percent, to $13.6 billion from $81.8 billion; Alphabet and Meta have repurchased nothing at all this year, Amazon has not bought back stock since 2022, and Microsoft accounted for nearly all of what remained.

The money went to AI instead. Capital spending by the five doubled to $556.9 billion in nine months — more than their entire operating cash flow of $542.9 billion, itself a record. Amazon alone spent $75.9 billion in the third quarter, nearly 80 percent more than the cash it generated, and raised $48.1 billion in long-term debt to help cover the gap.

That arithmetic is the real engine behind this week's market selloff: investors are being asked to fund the largest build-out in corporate history with cash that used to come back to them, on the promise that returns arrive later. Fund managers quoted by Reuters describe a generation-long shift in how big tech treats surplus cash — dividends and buybacks were the deal for 15 years; now the deal is data centers.

Watch the next two quarters of free cash flow. If spending keeps outrunning cash generation, expect louder shareholder pressure — and more days like Friday.

items.title: Americans expect an AI boom — just not one with jobs in it
items.summary:
The first Axios–CivicScience AI Sentiment Index, published Friday, puts a number on the country's split mood about artificial intelligence: Americans are broadly optimistic that AI will grow the economy, and deeply skeptical that it will be good for jobs, careers or everyday quality of life. The monthly index tracks six measures of public opinion, covering AI's effects on growth, society, jobs and quality of life, plus support for continued development and for building new data centers.

The underlying polling is pointed. A quarter of employed adults say they are very concerned about how AI could affect their careers, and among people in technical roles the figure is 40 percent — the workers closest to the technology are the most worried about it. The reading also matches the market's moment: the index launches the same week investors knocked roughly $2 trillion off the Nasdaq over doubts about AI spending.

Politically, AI opinion is starting to sort by party, with an Axios Harris Poll in late October showing diverging partisan views of AI companies. That makes the index worth watching as a monthly series — it could become the consumer-confidence number for the AI era, and a problem for both parties if the 'growth without jobs' mood hardens.

The next release lands in late November; watch whether the jobs measure keeps sliding as layoff headlines accumulate.

items.title: Record king tides keep flooding both coasts, with advisories running through Sunday
items.summary:
Exceptionally high king tides have flooded coastal communities from Southern California to South Florida all week, and the National Weather Service has extended coastal flood advisories around San Francisco, San Pablo and Monterey bays through November 1. Huntington Beach has declared a local emergency, stretches of Pacific Coast Highway have closed, and seawater has pushed into streets, homes and businesses.

The numbers are records, not nuisances: a San Diego gauge topped 8 feet, nearly a foot and a half above prediction, and Los Angeles Harbor set water-level records on consecutive days. King tides are the year's highest predictable tides, and scientists use weeks like this one as a preview of ordinary high-tide flooding as sea levels rise — what required an exceptional tide this week becomes a monthly event in the projections.

There is no storm behind this; it is astronomy plus elevated baseline water levels, which is exactly why emergency managers treat it as a planning exercise for the future as much as a cleanup job today.

The advisories run through Sunday, November 1. If you know anyone traveling to the California or South Florida coasts this weekend, tell them to check local flood closures before driving near the water at high tide.

items.title: Pope Leo XIV casts a mail ballot in the midterms — a first for a sitting pope
items.summary:
Pope Leo XIV has voted in the U.S. midterm elections, the Vatican confirmed Friday, submitting a mail-in ballot to Chicago — making him the first pope known to have voted in a U.S. election, and likely the first sitting pontiff to vote in any secular democratic election. The Holy See Press Office said Leo 'has exercised his right to vote as a United States citizen whenever he was eligible to do so,' and described the ballot as a continuation of a long-standing practice of civic participation.

Leo, born Robert Francis Prevost in Chicago, is registered in New Lenox, a suburb where his brother lives. He requested the ballot on October 3, ten days before undergoing surgery to remove a cancerous tumor from his right lung, and has been slowly resuming activities since leaving the hospital on October 17. Illinois records show he has voted in five primaries since 2000, requesting Democratic ballots twice and Republican ballots three times; the Vatican did not say which candidates he chose this time, on a ballot that includes Governor JB Pritzker's re-election and the open Senate seat left by Dick Durbin's retirement.

The vote lands in the middle of an open feud: Trump has repeatedly criticized Leo for condemning the U.S.–Israel war on Iran and the administration's immigration crackdown, and the pope in April urged Americans to contact their representatives to de-escalate the conflict. As head of the Vatican state he remains a U.S. citizen, and federal law lets citizens living abroad vote absentee — even, it turns out, citizens who run a foreign government.

The ballot still has to travel from Vatican City to Will County and arrive by the deadline to be counted — the county clerk said Thursday it had not yet arrived.

items.title: Early voting tops 49 million, a midterm record, with three days still to go
items.summary:
More than 49 million Americans have already voted in the midterms, according to the University of Florida's Election Lab — a record for a midterm, surpassing the roughly 46 million who had voted early by this point in 2022, with the final weekend of early voting and Election Day still ahead. The surge is being driven by early in-person voting, which keeps absorbing voters who used to vote by mail.

Ohio is a clean example of the shift: early in-person turnout has more than doubled in counties like Hamilton compared with 2022, while mail requests have fallen, and affiliated Democrats have made up a larger share of the early electorate than in past cycles — including in counties that backed Trump heavily. Both parties caution against reading results into who votes early, since Republicans have spent two cycles urging their voters to bank ballots early too.

The practical effect is a shorter Election Day: with this many votes already in, Tuesday is increasingly about turning out the remaining slice — and about counting, since states that cannot process mail ballots early may still report late into the night.

Watch Sunday's final early-vote numbers, and your own plan: in Cuyahoga County, early voting runs 8 AM–4 PM today and 1–5 PM Sunday at 1803 Superior Avenue in Cleveland.

items.title: Alaska's Senate race now has subpoenas, a same-name candidate, and a fight over counting the votes
items.summary:
Federal prosecutors have issued dozens of subpoenas in an investigation into whether Democrats recruited Daniel Jay Sullivan — a retired schoolteacher from a remote fishing village — to run for the U.S. Senate in Alaska specifically because he shares a name with Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan. The Justice Department has also asked a federal court, in an emergency filing, to order Alaska to segregate ballots in the race, seeking a ruling by Monday, four days before the election.

The department's top prosecutor in Alaska, U.S. Attorney Michael Heyman, laid out the 'sham candidate' allegation at a Friday press conference, acting on a civil lawsuit President Trump says he instigated. The department is separately trying to block the state from certifying the result if the incumbent loses a close race on a ballot carrying both Sullivans.

Look-alike candidate schemes are an old trick in American politics, but a federal criminal investigation and a pre-election ballot-segregation order in a race that could decide Senate control is new territory — and it arrives alongside a judge's order the same day barring the department from threatening election officials in other states.

Watch for the court's answer on segregation by Monday, and for how Alaska election officials instruct voters holding two Sullivans on one ballot.

items.title: U.S. sets travel restrictions tied to Congo's Ebola outbreak starting November 3
items.summary:
The U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention is putting a 21-day travel restriction policy in place for people traveling from the Democratic Republic of Congo, effective November 3 through December 18, as that country's Ebola outbreak passes 10,000 cases and 5,000 deaths. The measures respond to an epidemic caused by the Bundibugyo strain of Ebola, which has no approved vaccine or treatment and is spreading largely outside monitored contact chains.

Airline associations have also asked the CDC to reconsider Ebola declaration requirements for travelers, arguing the rules need to be workable for carriers while the screening net is up. Confirmed cases have been reported in Kenya, Uganda, Nigeria and France, and Saudi Arabia has suspended travel to and from Kenya — a reminder that the response is now global, not regional.

For most Americans this changes nothing about daily life; the outbreak's center is in eastern Congo, and U.S. screening is aimed at the small number of routes connecting the region to the United States. The bigger risk public-health officials cite is funding: the Africa CDC warns the response is short of the staff and money needed to trace contacts, which is how outbreaks like this actually end.

Watch the November 3 start date and any CDC updates to the country list as case reports come in over the next two weeks.
items.source: Wall Street Next / Africa CDC reports

items.title: Acton and Ramaswamy close out a bruising Ohio governor's race, with Acton narrowly ahead
items.summary:
Ohio's governor's race — one of seven governorships Reuters flags as the ones to watch Tuesday — is closing as one of the nastiest in the country. Democrat Amy Acton, the physician who led Ohio's pandemic response as health director, holds a narrow lead over Republican Vivek Ramaswamy: about 48 to 45 in the FiftyPlusOne polling average, and 48 to 44 in a Suffolk University/USA Today Network poll this week. Either winner makes history — Ohio's first woman governor, or its first governor of color.

The race's ugliest moment, an attack ad featuring Acton's estranged mother disputing her account of her childhood, was pulled by the Ramaswamy campaign after bipartisan criticism — Governor Mike DeWine condemned the ad while continuing to endorse Ramaswamy. Ramaswamy spent the final days rolling out seven Day One executive orders (next story) and hammering property taxes; Acton is rallying in Cleveland on Sunday on a promise to fully fund public schools, cut taxes for working Ohioans and break decades of Republican control of state government.

Ohio has backed Trump for a decade, so an Acton win would be a genuine earthquake — and polls show tight races down the ballot too, including the U.S. Senate fight between incumbent Jon Husted and Sherrod Brown, which is why national money and attention keep pouring in.

Final rallies Sunday — Ramaswamy in Canfield, Acton in Cleveland — then polls Tuesday, 6:30 AM to 7:30 PM.

items.title: Ramaswamy unveils seven Day One executive orders, from property-tax probes to a data-center pause
items.summary:
Vivek Ramaswamy has published the seven executive orders he says he would sign on his first day as governor, January 11, 2027, if he wins Tuesday. The list: investigations into every locality where property taxes have more than doubled since 2020; ending sanctuary cities across Ohio; pausing new data-center projects until the legislature passes comprehensive data-center legislation; a crackdown on Medicaid fraud; a violent-crime enforcement push; a sweep for wasteful bureaucratic spending; and a new inter-agency anti-fraud task force answering directly to the governor, alongside a state task force on visa fraud.

The property-tax plank is the campaign's closing argument. Ramaswamy has called Ohio's property-tax burden a moral issue, arguing that people who own their homes outright should not face perpetual, escalating payments to keep them, and has promised homeowners 'the truth' about how the money is spent. The data-center pause is aimed at a live local fight — communities across Ohio are split over the power and water demands of the AI build-out.

These are campaign pledges, not law: they take effect only if Ramaswamy wins, and several would need the legislature or the courts to hold up. But the list is a useful map of what a Ramaswamy administration would try first.

Watch Tuesday's result — and, if he wins, how much of the seven survives contact with the General Assembly in January.

items.title: Republicans pour millions into saving Max Miller in a once-safe Cleveland-area House seat
items.summary:
Ohio's 7th Congressional District — stretching from Cleveland's outer suburbs into rural counties beyond, in territory Trump won by 11 points — was supposed to be safe Republican ground. Instead, national Republicans have poured millions into saving Rep. Max Miller in the closing weeks, after quietly trying earlier this year to push him out of the race entirely. Miller has loaned his own campaign $1.25 million as donor fundraising lagged, raising just $145,000 from donors last quarter.

The trouble is personal as much as political. Miller's ex-wife has alleged abuse during their marriage, including that he held a gun to her when their daughter was an infant — claims he vehemently denies. His former father-in-law, U.S. Sen. Bernie Moreno, publicly said Miller should not serve in Congress, as did fellow Ohio Sen. Jon Husted. Miller refused to step aside before the August replacement deadline, telling CNN he has 'the utmost confidence that my constituents back home know me.' A custody trial over his daughter is scheduled to begin just days after Election Day, whichever way the vote goes.

In a year when voters everywhere are punishing incumbents over prices, a scandal-damaged incumbent in red territory is exactly the kind of seat that turns a bad night into a wave. House control could come down to a net of three seats, so this race counts far beyond the district.

Watch the 7th District on Tuesday night — it is an early-warning seat: if Miller is struggling, Republicans are struggling everywhere.

items.title: Browns get their defensive tackles back together for Sunday's first-place showdown in Pittsburgh
items.summary:
For the first time since October 1, the Browns expect to have defensive tackles Mason Graham and Mike Hall Jr. on the field together Sunday in Pittsburgh, in a game between two 5-2 teams for first place in the AFC North. Both were hurt in the first half of the Browns' Week 4 win over these same Steelers — Graham with a sprained MCL and ankle, Hall with a sprained ankle — and have spent weeks rehabbing side by side. 'We were kind of in there in the training room for a few weeks working it out,' Graham said Friday. 'We're both happy to be back out there.'

Hall's return matters beyond the reunion. He played through the injury in that first Steelers game and still recorded a sack, and his presence addresses the Browns' most glaring recent weakness, run defense. Cleveland's pass rush is already producing — seventh in the league with 20 sacks and sixth in sack rate — and Pittsburgh quarterback Aaron Rodgers has been sacked 22 times this season, third-most in the NFL. The Browns won the first meeting 27–24 on Andre Szmyt's career-long 56-yard field goal with 10 seconds left. The pregame edge has already started: safety Grant Delpit spent Friday mocking the playing surface at Acrisure Stadium.

Kickoff is Sunday at 1 PM on CBS. A win puts Cleveland alone atop the division heading into the season's second half.

items.title: Final weekend of early voting in Cuyahoga County — and check your polling place, 66 precincts moved
items.summary:
Early in-person voting for Tuesday's general election wraps up this weekend at the Cuyahoga County Board of Elections, 1803 Superior Avenue in Cleveland: today, Saturday, from 8:00 AM to 4:00 PM, and the final session Sunday, November 1, from 1:00 PM to 5:00 PM. After that, the only way to vote is at your precinct on Election Day, Tuesday, when polls are open 6:30 AM to 7:30 PM. Mail ballots must be returned by 7:30 PM on Election Night, and the board advises allowing the Postal Service at least seven days — at this point, drop a mail ballot off in person instead.

One warning worth passing around the family group chat: the board announced this week that 66 precincts in 9 cities have changed locations, affecting nearly 60,000 voters, and staff have been touring libraries across Cleveland's wards to spread the word. If you vote on Election Day, confirm your location on the board's site before you drive anywhere. The board also reported that an unidentified powder found in a returned mail ballot on October 28 was tested and determined to be non-hazardous, with normal processing continuing.

Ohio's early vote is running hot — in-person early turnout has more than doubled in several counties compared with 2022 — and with the governor's race, a U.S. Senate race and every statewide office on the ballot, Cuyahoga County expects a busy Tuesday.

Today 8–4 or Sunday 1–5 at Superior Avenue beats a Tuesday line. Bring an accepted ID, and double-check your precinct if you are waiting for Election Day.

items.title: Cleveland driver indicted on murder charge in the hit-and-run death of cyclist Frank Mays
items.summary:
Cuyahoga County Prosecutor Michael O'Malley announced Friday that Tyrelle Taylor has been indicted on charges including murder and involuntary manslaughter in the October 18 hit-and-run death of bicyclist William 'Frank' Mays, 35. Prosecutors say Taylor, driving a black 2010 Ford F-150 Raptor downtown on West 6th Street that Sunday afternoon, fled from Cleveland police officers who tried to stop him on foot, struck multiple vehicles as he drove off, then veered into the marked bike lane on the right shoulder near West 25th Street and hit Mays, who was riding in the lane.

Mays was found in the grass behind the truck and taken to the hospital, where he was pronounced dead about 90 minutes after being struck. Taylor turned himself in on October 21 and was arrested by U.S. Marshals and Cleveland police. The indictment, returned October 30, charges one count of murder and one count of involuntary manslaughter among other counts; an arraignment date at the Cuyahoga County Justice Center has not yet been set.

The case has become a focal point for Cleveland cyclists and downtown safety advocates, in part because the fatal stretch is a clearly marked, green-painted bike lane on a street where officers were already posted directing traffic.

Watch for the arraignment date and whether prosecutors seek to hold Taylor without bond pending trial.

baby.tip: Do the final hospital-bag sweep together this weekend: IDs and insurance cards in the front pocket, phone chargers and a long cable, snacks for Mike, and a going-home outfit for the baby in newborn and 0–3 month sizes — babies pick their own size. Then leave the bag by the door, not in a closet, so nobody is packing at 3 AM.
baby.fact: Newborns see best at about 8 to 12 inches from their face — almost exactly the distance to a parent's face during a feed — and they already recognize their mother's voice from hearing it in the womb. High-contrast black-and-white patterns are the first 'pictures' a new baby can really study.
